Fun fact — egg size isn’t only dependent on chicken breed and their feed. The same chicken can lay larger eggs and smaller eggs.

I have three hens. Two tend to lay large eggs and one tends to lay small eggs, but sometimes the two lay small eggs and the one lays a huge egg. (If you have a small number of chickens it’s easy to learn which chicken is laying what egg based on the shade of the shell and whether the shell has any speckles on it). The eggs of the two are fairly round, and the eggs of the one are fairly pointy. 

Why? Don’t know. Just sharing a random bit of chicken knowledge.

Author: @SwordGuardian
Content:
I remember doing the 150th reenactment of 1st Manassass.  It was... amazingly similar to the actual battle, in all the worst ways.

  Temperatures rose to around 100ºF with high humidity, so sweat didn't evaporate and fans just blew hot air over you.  People came from all over the country to see it, but the line of cars clogged up the roads.  When people started dropping left and right from the heat, the ambulances, some coming from as far as Washington D.C., struggled to get in through the 1 dirt road leading to the battlefield.  The biggest difference was that we had ATVs coming out mid-battle to give ice and bottled water to folks, which reenactors know to put the ice in their hats.

  Surprisingly enough, most of the people that needed medical attention were the civilian spectators.  Ironically, our wool uniforms provided good protection from direct sunlight, and wicked moisture from the skin, plus wool breathes well.  Even so, the best of us were uncomfortable, and many people still had heat exhaustion.  My brother turned as red as a tomato in the heat.

  When all was said and done, there were over 100 people needing some degree of medical attention, dozens taken to the hospital, several people biten by snakes (Later identfied to be non-venomous, but more aggressive with the heat) 1 lady with a bee allergy stung, and, according to rumor, as many as 4 killed by heat stroke.(One official source said while the event was still ongoing that 3 died, but the same source later said no one died at the event.  I do know that sometimes people want to cover up severity, and will use the technicallity that they aren't legally dead until a doctor, usually at a hospital, calls it.  The question to ask would be "how many people from the reenactment died at the hospitals" but even then, it wouldn't surprise me one way or another, if it was 0 or if it was 20 makes little difference.)

  Regardless of the outcome, no one would deny that the organization of that particular reenactment was awful, as were the atmospheric conditions.

Author: @Azerinth
Content:
6:36 A trick for buttering and flouring the pans, if you use either wax paper, (like what the butter is likely wrapped in) or a paper towel, you can get a more even and thorough covering. Then put a couple tablespoons of flour in the pan, and seal it with Plastic Wrap. Turn the pan around in the air and tap gently, so the pile of flour moves around and covers the sides and edges. If the flour doesn't stick somewhere, it means you missed while greasing. 
Once you have it all covered, turn the pan upside down on a counter and unbind the plastic wrap. Tap the pan and lift it off and you'll have a fully floured pan with all the excess flour neatly contained in the plastic wrap to be disposed of.

Author: @HikuroMishiro
Content: I think something that people leave out about Fort Sumpter is that from South Carolina's perspective another nation is occupying their fort and refused to leave and once additional men and supplies were on the way they were forced to escalate the situation. There were also no fatalities as a result of the battle. Had diplomatic tactics gone differently the battle could have been avoided, or alternatively it could have been the first and last battle. Lincoln's call for 75,000 additional men to crush the rebellion was a primary factor in getting four other states to secede and join the Confederacy. So while there's possibly some truth to 'a war at some point was inevitable' there are also a lot of different ways things could have gone.

Author: @hollandsemum1
Content:
The original little stone bridge across the river, down the hill from the farmhouse is still there. At the battle of Waterloo, they had a full blown ball the night before, in a nearby town.

I've been baking pound cake from scratch for decades, from a European recipe from the 20th century.
The instruction she gives is not the one you give. The one from my cookbook agrees with hers. You *do* need to beat the butter a fair bit to get it soft as cream. That would be the consistency of risen fresh or clotted cream. That means beating it until the color goes pale, and it's been aerated to triple the original volume a tasting spoon of it will show a great difference in the texture, which will in turn allow better mixing, and a lighter cake (It's also what is used for basic buttercream to keep it light & fluffy). Then you add the sugar beating until it's fluffy. The reason she has the eggs prepped by beating until foamy is because it loosens the whites & yolks for consistent mixing in. Today we accomplish it by beating the eggs in one at a time and scraping between each addtion. If you rely strictly on the eggs for air, you'd need to make a genoise to get a light cake - tough to do without the yolks separating out. In this case, it is beating the butter that provides & maintains air. The one thing they do have in common is to be gentle mixing in the flour. 
You do consistently good research on the recipe content, but periodically the understanding of pre appliance technique and how it's described, isn't quite interpreted as well, leading to some of the subtle problems encountered (though you definitely have fermentation down well 😁 - *cough* garum *cough*).

Author: @cowboyfrankspersonalvideos8869
Content:
The official name is 'Manassas National Battlefield Park".  Most of the battles in the south were named by a nearby river or stream. The battles in the north tended to have names of the nearest cities. Manassas is (I believe) the only National Park in the south, dealing with the civil war which got the city name. 
During the late 1990s, I was a volunteer at Manassas. Mostly I took care of their computers but started building their website in 1995. That site ended up being the first web page for any National Park in the World, and I'm greatly proud of that title. I still have that website on one of my web accounts. 
On the section dealing with the battles, I have two, silent, YouTube videos extracted from 8mm movie film about the one and only "reenactment" which occurred at any US National Park location. The battle was a mess. More information, photos and the videos can be found on this linked page.

http://nps-vip.net/history/1961/index.htm

Author: @johnbaker6125
Content:
CSA General P.G.T. Beauregard is a pretty fascinating figure that has mostly been forgotten about. He was the first official general of the confederate army resigning his post as commandant of West Point the day he took it. He ordered the shots that started the war, participated in many major battles in both the Eastern and Western campaign, urged the development of the Confederate Battle Flag and attracted women wherever he went. It was the fact that he was considered attractive to women, including many other officer's wives, that many believe that was partially why he was more or less demoted to being a secondary General even when officially he was the 5th major general as time went on as well as having Creole descent. He had a dark olive skin tone, spoke with a French accent and many considered him a "foreigner". He was even the target of racial slurs after the war when the tensions over Reconstruction were at their height.

After the war the Freedman's Bureau took all his land holdings east of downtown Memphis, he became very bitter. He later had a change of heart, became a widely respected public servant in his home state of Louisianna and was actually an early civil rights activist for freed blacks. He advocated for reconciliation with the North, suffrage rights for freedmen and equal treatment for all the people of Louisianna. He was widely respected throughout the country in his later years often being invited to speak throughout the country. When he died a black creole poet known for writing poems about early civil rights leaders wrote an epithet to him showering his life with praises.

And in New Orleans, they tore his statue down before they did Lee's.

Author: @josephhargrove4319
Content:
First Bull Run/Manassas (which was much closer to Washington D.C. than to Richmond) could have had the effect predicted by the Southern press, but the southern army was as green and undisciplined as the northern army. After driving the northern army from the field, they stopped to rest, loot, eat, etc., and the officers who recognized the opportunity lying in their laps (advance and take Washington D.C. which was essentially defenseless) could not get their army organized to push their advantage to completion. The battle literally put the fear of God into Lincoln who spent the remainder of the war bolstering the defenses around Washington D.C. and drilling it into his generals that they must defend Washington at all costs. Meade, a competent if conservative general, geared his movements in Pennsylvania to keep the Army of the Potomac between the Army of Northern Virginia and Washington. An historical aside: Meade, unlike all the previous commanders,  was never relieved of command of the Army of the Potomac. His command just became a part of Grant's larger force.

Author: @hamburgerlord7849
Content:
Fun Fact, during the 90's Disney wanted to build a new theme park a few miles out from the Bull Run battle site, called "Disney's America". The park would have a recreation of the different areas of American history, from a native village and 1776 Boston all the way to a WW2 airstrip. And yes, they would have recreated the Battle of Bull Run not 10 miles away from the actual site. Initially, interest in the smaller regional park was high, but soon a bunch of historians came out to protest against Disney... Disney-fying American history. And while thier depiction would have been leagues more accurate than Walt Disney's original Liberty Street at Disneyland (and way less racist) it was still a concern. Ultimately the project was canned when it was revealed the park would be on top of some other civil war historic sites in the area.

One of the funniest things to come from this era, though, was a national hearing between the state of Virginia and Disney against the protestors. One of the protesters opened his argument by saying "I'm not here to argue if Mickey Mouse would have worn a blue or grey uniform", and I just think that's a really funny way to address a national audience out of context

Author: @ericbarlow6772
Content:
I used to live about 20-30 minutes from the 1st and 2nd Manassas Battlefield (yes, I grew up in the South and use their nomenclature for some of the battles). I think it’s funny how we even disagree on the names. Im sorry but calling it Bull Run just sounds like bull to my ears 

We got here because in Union dispatches, they would typically use the closest landmark (Bull Run, Antietam, Ball’s Bluff) while Confederate dispatches would use the closest town (Manassas, Sharpsburg, Leesburg). 

My family is part of the history, especially on my father’s side. My great X 3 grandfather was conscripted into the Confederate Army, deserted and joined the Union Army in Knoxville while his brother fought for the Confederate Army. My grandfather survived the war; however, the brother was mortally wounded at Spotsylvania Courthouse and sent home to North Wilkesboro, NC to die with his family.
